messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samir was twenty-two when the assault happened in the narrow, poorly lit service corridor of a downtown conference center. The air had been thick with the cloying scent of synthetic leather and spilled coffee, and he remembered the sudden, sharp lunge of his attacker, the blur of motion that left him pinned and paralyzed, and the humiliating, deliberate words that followed. In the months that followed, his body remained constantly on guard against unseen danger, so much so that ordinary olfactory cues and the sudden shift of a stranger’s shoulders immediately pulled him back into the corridor’s memory, his heart hammering as if the violation were happening again. As an auditor, his job required him to move between client offices, review ledgers, and present findings in glass-walled conference rooms, but the professional environment quickly became a minefield. Whenever a colleague made a passing remark about his dating life, or when he witnessed two people arguing aggressively over expense reports, the sense of moral violation and relationship reminder surged through him. These moments fractured his sense of self, leading him to compare himself to the confident men he saw at networking events, mourn the loss of his old happiness, and settle into a conviction that he was permanently humiliated. Because these triggers consistently chipped away at his self-worth, Samir began altering his daily habits. He started wearing heavy, high-collared sweaters even in heated boardrooms, deliberately positioning himself near the door during client meetings, and refusing to participate in any workplace activity where his appearance or performance might be scrutinized. Convinced he was fundamentally compromised by what happened, he kept his clothes concealing and steered clear of any situation where he might be evaluated. The cycle tightened with relentless efficiency. Because his body felt constantly on guard against unseen danger, he defaulted to staying near the exits of every room and refusing to enter unfamiliar spaces where he could not assess the threat. By hiding in oversized layers and dodging evaluation, he convinced himself that he was permanently humiliated and that his capacity for joy was gone forever. The more he adopted these protective habits, the more acutely he noticed the scent of synthetic leather on passing strangers and the casual remarks of colleagues about their pasts, which immediately reinforced his belief that the world was fundamentally unsafe. Worse, his relentless efforts to control his environment only kept his nervous system locked in high alert, ensuring that his tension never broke. Every concealing layer he wore and every avoided social gathering fed his hypervigilance, binding him to a silent, exhausting routine that left him isolated from friends and increasingly unable to meet his audit deadlines. What finally drove Samir to the clinic was a panic attack in the elevator of his firm’s headquarters. He had been alone, but the sudden drop in pressure and the faint whiff of an older man’s cologne had triggered a wave of suffocating dread that left him pressed against the corner wall, unable to move or breathe. Sitting in the intake room now, Samir admitted that he was terrified of his own body, afraid that if he stopped monitoring every exit and every scent, the humiliation would consume him entirely. What he hoped for, though, was the chance to step out of the service corridor and finally feel safe in his own skin.
